evals.prompt: We have a major football match streaming live in 6 weeks — expected peak about 8x our daily baseline, and the critical path (auth, manifest generation, ad decisioning, playback) runs on EKS in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Walk us through a large-scale live event readiness review for this: what to check across each readiness area, what good looks like, and where the risks are — as a graded readiness plan we can work through before the event.
evals.expected_output: A structured readiness review organized across the nine readiness pillars (Capacity & Scaling, Service Quotas, Resilience, Content Delivery, Networking, Data & State, Testing & Chaos, Observability, Operational Readiness & Support). For each pillar it states what to verify and what good looks like, assigns a severity to each risk, uses PASS/FAIL/N/A verdicts (N/A where live resource data is not available), frames the work against the weeks-to-event capacity-planning timeline, and ends with a severity-ranked, timeline-mapped action plan. Remediations are proposals for human approval; the response performs no changes and reserves or pre-warms nothing.
assertions: Frames the review against weeks-to-event — what must happen by when on the capacity-planning timeline (e.g. 12-16 weeks out vs the final week)

Findings are organized across the readiness pillars (at least capacity/scaling, service quotas, resilience, content delivery, networking, data/state, testing, observability, and support) rather than a flat list
Any gap it identifies carries a severity level (Critical/High/Medium/Low) and the action plan is ordered by severity
Capacity guidance emphasizes pre-provisioning over reactive autoscaling (for example instance diversification, On-Demand Capacity Reservations, or pre-warming), not autoscaling alone
Produces a severity-ranked action plan (Critical -> Low) with each gap tied to a capacity-planning milestone, rather than an unordered list of recommendations

evals.prompt: We use Karpenter on EKS, DynamoDB and Amazon Keyspaces for session/state, and ElastiCache; our daily baseline is small but the event will spike hard. What capacity preparation should we have in place for the event, and what does good look like for this stack — covering how to absorb a sharp spike rather than relying on reactive autoscaling?
evals.expected_output: Capacity-readiness guidance covering: instance diversification across families/sizes/AZs and On-Demand Capacity Reservations (including future-dated reservations for the event); EKS control-plane / Karpenter pre-provisioning; for the data stores, checking DynamoDB and Keyspaces warm throughput against the projected peak and pre-warming (raising warm throughput) or provisioning to peak only where warm throughput falls short — noting that an on-demand table previously provisioned high already covers the peak; pre-warming or pre-sizing ElastiCache ahead of the ramp; and raising pre-provisioned minimum capacity rather than relying on reactive autoscaling. Actions are presented as proposals for the user to perform.
assertions: For DynamoDB and Amazon Keyspaces, checks warm throughput against the projected peak — pre-warming (raising warm throughput) or provisioning to peak only where it falls short — rather than blanket pre-warming or treating on-demand as automatically cold
Covers On-Demand Capacity Reservations, including future-dated reservations for the event
Notes that reactive autoscaling alone is insufficient for a sharp spike and recommends pre-provisioned minimum capacity
Presents pre-warm and capacity-reservation steps as actions for the user to take, not changes it has made

evals.prompt: Audit our Amazon CloudFront and origin setup for a big live streaming event. Our live segments are 4 seconds.
evals.expected_output: A content-delivery review that checks delivery through CloudFront with a single consistent origin, whether Origin Shield is enabled for origin offload, cache-key normalization and stripping query-string variation to keep a high cache-hit ratio on short-TTL (2-6s) live segments, the correct split between CloudFront Functions and Lambda@Edge, and origin failover.
assertions: Explains that short-TTL live segments (2-6 seconds) make origin offload critical, and recommends Origin Shield to keep the origin request rate predictable at peak
Addresses cache-key normalization or stripping query-string variation to protect the cache-hit ratio on short-TTL live segments
Recommends CloudFront Functions for lightweight, high-frequency edge logic and Lambda@Edge for heavier runtime work
Recommends designing for a high cache-hit ratio on the short-TTL live segments, for example a single consistent origin and normalized cache keys

evals.prompt: Before our live event, how do we prove the platform will hold? What load and chaos testing should we have done?
evals.expected_output: A testing plan describing the staged gates (component, integration, a full-scale production rehearsal at roughly 1.3-1.5x expected peak, and spike-and-failure testing), a realistic ramp profile rather than zero-to-peak, the identity/signup surge test and the ad-decisioning path test that a media-pipeline scale test does not cover, and AWS Fault Injection Service experiments with stop conditions and steady state defined in viewer terms (video start time, rebuffering ratio, error rate).
assertions: Describes staged load testing including a full-scale production rehearsal at roughly 1.3-1.5x expected peak
Gives a concrete ramp shape - roughly a 60-minute ramp to peak, a 2-3 hour sustain with periodic 20-40% spikes, then decline - not just a vague 'ramp gradually'
Calls out the identity/signup surge test and the ad-decisioning path test as things a media-pipeline scale test will not catch
Defines steady state in viewer terms such as video start time, rebuffering ratio, or error rate
Recommends AWS Fault Injection Service experiments with automatic stop conditions that halt the experiment when viewer impact exceeds a threshold

evals.prompt: Our live event is in 4 days. Quick readiness check - can we still fix everything in time?
evals.expected_output: A readiness check that recognizes the short lead time and distinguishes items that can still be remediated from residual risk that cannot (manual quota increases needing AWS coordination, future-dated On-Demand Capacity Reservations, and AWS Support pre-warms), and offers day-of mitigations such as widening instance diversification or raising minimum capacity. It still performs no changes.
assertions: Acknowledges the lead time is too short to fully remediate some items
Flags manual quota increases, future-dated capacity reservations, and Support pre-warms as residual risk rather than fixable in time
Offers day-of mitigations such as widening instance diversification or raising minimum capacity
Prioritizes the few highest-impact actions still achievable in the remaining days rather than a full multi-week remediation program

evals.prompt: Readiness check on observability for our live event. We don't use CloudWatch alarms — all our alerting runs through Datadog. Critical path is auth, manifest, and playback on EKS in us-east-1. This is a one-shot check — assume typical event values where needed and give me the observability assessment now, don't wait for more detail.
evals.expected_output: An observability-pillar assessment that grades alarm coverage tool-agnostically: it does not FAIL the platform purely because CloudWatch alarms are absent when Datadog is the declared alerting platform, confirms each critical-path service (auth, manifest, playback) has an actionable alarm routed to on-call, recognizes that third-party alarm coverage cannot be verified through read-only AWS access and asks for manual confirmation rather than assuming, and still flags any critical-path service with no alarm in any tool as a gap with a severity.
assertions: Delivers a structured alarm-coverage verdict (PASS/FAIL/N/A with a severity) and marks the absence of CloudWatch alarms as N/A/expected under the declared Datadog-only alerting model, rather than an automatic FAIL or generic prose

Takes a per-critical-service view (auth, manifest, playback) and, where coverage cannot be verified via read-only AWS access, names the specific services the user must confirm are alarmed in the third-party tool
Marks third-party (Datadog) alarm coverage N/A — explicitly not PASS — because read-only AWS access cannot inspect it, and requests manual confirmation rather than assuming coverage
States the rule that a critical-path service with no actionable alarm in any tool would be a FAIL carrying a severity, even though here coverage is N/A pending Datadog confirmation

evals.prompt: We're prepping a big live match. Capacity is sorted but I'm not sure our operational readiness is there — do we have the right success criteria and an event-day plan? Give me the assessment now; assume typical event values where you need to and note the assumptions.
evals.expected_output: An operational-readiness assessment that checks for measurable glass-to-glass success criteria with a warning/critical/failure KPI threshold matrix signed off by stakeholders (e.g. VPF, video start time, rebuffer, uptime) and a documented, rehearsed event-day communication plan — a Comms Manager, per-team designated reporters on a fixed update cadence, and bridge etiquette — presented as readiness checks, making no changes.
assertions: Grades measurable success criteria as a check with a PASS/FAIL/N/A verdict and severity, naming specific glass-to-glass KPIs (e.g. VPF, video start time, rebuffer, uptime) and a warning/critical/failure threshold matrix — not merely advising that KPIs are useful
Recommends a documented, rehearsed event-day communication plan with defined roles (Comms Manager, designated reporters) and a fixed update cadence
Flags the absence of documented, stakeholder-signed-off success criteria as a graded gap/risk carrying a severity, rather than only noting it would be good to have
Frames findings as a readiness scorecard with per-item PASS/FAIL/N/A verdicts, each gap mapped to a remediation, rather than freeform prose advice

evals.prompt: Readiness check for ads and DRM on our live sports event. We use AWS Elemental MediaTailor for server-side ad insertion with scheduled breaks at halftime and quarter changes, and the stream is DRM-protected (Widevine + PlayReady + FairPlay) via a third-party license server behind SPEKE. This is a one-shot check — assume typical event values and give me the readiness assessment now, don't wait for more detail.
evals.expected_output: A graded readiness assessment covering: MediaTailor playback configuration (CDN7) — in particular whether PrefetchSchedule is defined for the scheduled ad breaks so the ADS is called ahead of the viewer surge rather than under it, and whether the player degrades gracefully (slate / resumes content) when the ADS is slow or unavailable; ADS/VAST endpoint capacity confirmed with the vendor at projected QPS (TST4) and ad-tracking beacon pipeline sized for peak (OBS6); DRM license-server capacity confirmed with the SPEKE key provider at projected peak license-request rate (DAT7), with staggered key-renewal windows so renewals don't cluster, and player-side token caching. Produces PASS/FAIL/N/A verdicts with severity and remediations; makes no changes.
assertions: Grades MediaTailor readiness as a check with PASS/FAIL/N/A and severity, naming PrefetchSchedule for scheduled ad breaks (halftime / quarter changes) and the player's slate / graceful-degradation fallback when the ADS is slow or unavailable

Separately treats the ADS/VAST endpoint capacity as a check — confirmed with the vendor at projected peak QPS with the timeout budget held — rather than conflating it with MediaTailor service capacity

Grades DRM readiness (DAT7) as a check with PASS/FAIL/N/A and severity, naming the third-party license-server capacity (confirmed with the SPEKE key provider), staggered key-renewal windows, and player-side DRM token caching
Flags ad-tracking beacon pipeline (impression / quartile / completion pixels) load-testing at peak concurrency as part of the ad-decisioning readiness, not only the ad decision itself

evals.prompt: We stream a weekly live show on Amazon IVS (the turn-key low-latency service, not MediaLive + MediaPackage + CloudFront). We have an upcoming high-profile episode — is this skill the right fit, and if so what does a readiness review look like for an IVS-based platform? One-shot assessment please.
evals.expected_output: An honest applicability call: Amazon IVS is a service-managed turn-key streaming stack, so most of the capacity / networking / CDN primitives this skill grades are AWS-managed and come up N/A. The response grades only the customer-managed portions — IVS service-quota headroom (RES7-style version/quota lifecycle), customer-managed state stores (DAT), observability against the IVS client SDK QoE metrics (OBS1), and operational readiness (SUP) as-is — and recommends an IVS-specific review for depth on the IVS primitives this skill doesn't cover. Produces PASS/FAIL/N/A verdicts and makes no changes.
assertions: Correctly recognises Amazon IVS as a service-managed turn-key stack and marks the AWS-managed primitives (CAP compute diversification, NAT/TGW networking, CloudFront CDN) as N/A rather than attempting to grade them against self-managed criteria

Still grades the customer-managed portions as checks with PASS/FAIL/N/A — customer-managed state stores, observability against IVS client SDK metrics, operational readiness and support engagement — rather than refusing the request entirely
Notes that a full IVS-primitive review requires an IVS-specific skill or vendor engagement, and that this skill's depth on the IVS service itself is reduced
Does not invent IVS-specific checks (e.g. does not claim to inspect IVS channel ingest settings it has no evidence for) — any un-verifiable item is N/A with a reason

evals.prompt: How do I configure AWS Elemental MediaLive and MediaPackage to encode and package a live channel?
Our live event is happening right now and viewers are seeing buffering - help me investigate the incident.
Write a Lambda function in Python that resizes images uploaded to an S3 bucket.
